historical_timeline.summary: Born at Woolsthorpe, Lincolnshire; his father had died before his birth.
Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge; Lucasian Professor from 1669; Fellow of the Royal Society from 1672.
Loss of appetite and want of sleep begin, by his biographer's account.
Writes to Pepys of his distress, poor sleep and appetite, and his withdrawal from friends.
Writes to Locke retracting his suspicions and asking forgiveness.
Tells a friend at Huntingdon that a distemper kept him awake five nights; apologizes to Pepys through him.
Explains to Locke that he had barely slept for a fortnight.
A second-hand report of insanity noted by Huygens; later disputed.
Master of the Mint; later President of the Royal Society.
Locke describes him as apt to raise suspicions where there is no ground.
Urinary incontinence; a bladder stone passed in 1724.
Dies at Kensington of a bladder stone, aged 84.
Retrospective proposals of mercury poisoning, manic-depressive illness, and Asperger's syndrome; all disputed.

claims.statement: Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe, in the parish of Colsterworth, Lincolnshire, on Christmas Day 1642 (25 December 1642 in the Julian calendar then used in England; 4 January 1643 in the Gregorian calendar), the only son of Isaac, a farmer, and his wife Hannah Ayscough. His father died before he was born, and his mother later remarried and had three more children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; the cause of his father's death is not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: He was educated at Grantham and at Trinity College, Cambridge, became a Fellow of Trinity in 1667, held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics from 1669 to 1702, and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1672.

His biographer David Brewster, working from Newton's manuscripts, wrote that he was deeply engaged in chemical experiments in December 1692 and January 1693. Among his papers is a one-page manuscript in his hand titled 'Notes on mercury and its purification'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His alchemical work with metals, including mercury, is documented; the amount of mercury he breathed or handled is not.

claims.statement: Brewster wrote that from the autumn of 1692 Newton complained of loss of appetite and want of sleep, which continued for nearly a twelvemonth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A nineteenth-century biographer's summary drawn from the letters that follow.

claims.statement: On 13 September 1693 (Julian; 23 September, Gregorian) Newton wrote to Samuel Pepys that he was 'extremely troubled at the embroilment I am in, and have neither ate nor slept well this twelvemonth, nor have my former consistency of mind', that he had never designed to get anything by Pepys's interest or the King's favour, and that he must withdraw from Pepys's acquaintance and see neither him nor the rest of his friends any more.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words; they record poor sleep and appetite, distress, and withdrawal, not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: On 16 September 1693 (Julian; 26 September, Gregorian), writing from the Bull in Shoreditch, London, he told John Locke that, being of opinion that Locke had endeavoured to embroil him with women and by other means, he had answered, when told Locke was sickly and would not live, that 'twere better if you were dead'. He begged Locke's pardon for this, for representing that Locke's book struck at the root of morality and taking him for a Hobbist, and for saying or thinking that there was a design to sell him an office or to embroil him; he signed himself Locke's 'most humble and unfortunate servant'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The letter records suspicions of a friend that he then retracted, and an apology; no threat or act of harm is recorded.

claims.statement: John Millington of Magdalene College wrote to Pepys on 30 September 1693 (Julian) that he had met Newton at Huntingdon on the 28th, when Newton, of his own accord, said he had written Pepys 'a very odd letter', in 'a distemper that much seized his head, and that kept him awake for above five nights together', and asked Millington to beg Pepys's pardon. Millington judged him now very well, though 'under some small degree of melancholy', with no reason to suspect that it had touched his understanding.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A friend's contemporary report of insomnia, low spirits, and apology.

claims.statement: Locke replied from Oates on 5 October 1693 (Julian) that he forgave Newton freely and fully. Newton answered from Cambridge on 15 October 1693 (Julian; 25 October, Gregorian) that the previous winter, by sleeping too often by his fire, he had got an ill habit of sleeping, that a distemper which that summer had been epidemical had put him further out of order, and that when he wrote he had not slept an hour a night for a fortnight together, and for five days together not a wink; he did not remember what he had said of Locke's book.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of severe insomnia.

claims.statement: The scientist Christiaan Huygens noted on 29 May 1694 that a Scotsman had told him that some eighteen months earlier Newton had become insane, from too intense application to his studies or from grief at losing his laboratory and manuscripts to fire, and that his friends had cared for him at home until he recovered. Brewster rejected the story, pointing to the letters and scholarly work Newton produced during that time.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A second-hand report noted in a private journal; its claims of insanity and confinement are not corroborated by the letters and are disputed by later biographers.

claims.statement: Brewster, in his 1855 biography, argued that Newton's mind was never in a state of derangement during 1692 and 1693; a reviewer of the following year judged that his own letters placed beyond doubt an illness that lamentably shook his nerves and, for a time, interfered with the coherent exercise of his faculties.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Nineteenth-century interpretations, opposed to each other.

claims.statement: In 1979 two papers in Notes and Records of the Royal Society proposed that mercury poisoning from his chemical and alchemical experiments explained his illness of 1692 and 1693: Johnson and Wolbarsht called it a probable cause of his physical and mental ills, and Spargo and Pounds reported that hairs attributed to him contained several heavy metals, including mercury, at concentrations much higher than in modern hair, which they offered as circumstantial evidence for the hypothesis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective hypothesis; the provenance and dating of the hair are uncertain and the evidence is circumstantial.

claims.statement: Other writers proposed manic-depressive illness rather than mercury poisoning (Lieb and Hershman, 1983). In 2008 Milo Keynes argued that the madness of 1692 and 1693 was due to mercury poisoning and not to clinical depression, and that Newton's lifelong distrust of others followed from his separation from his mother in childhood and not, as had been claimed, from Asperger's syndrome.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Competing retrospective interpretations; none can be tested, and none is used as a diagnosis in this record.

claims.statement: Locke remarked in 1703 that he had several reasons to think Newton truly his friend, but that he was 'a nice man to deal with, and a little too apt to raise in himself suspicions where there is no ground'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A friend's later description of his temperament.

claims.statement: Newton became Master of the Mint in 1699 and was President of the Royal Society from 1705 to 1727.

In 1722, in his eightieth year, he was seized with incontinence of urine, first ascribed to the stone and thought incurable, then attributed to a weakness of the bladder sphincter; his physician advised him to give up his carriage and dining out and to eat simply. In August 1724 he passed, without pain, a stone about the size of a pea, in two pieces some days apart; John Conduitt noted that he had voided two stones as big as a pea.

He fell ill on 3 March 1727 (Julian) after a visit to London. When John Conduitt learned of it on 11 March he sent for Dr Richard Mead and the surgeon William Cheselden, who pronounced the disease to be stone in the bladder and held out no hope of recovery. He had severe fits of pain, seemed easier on 15 March, became insensible on the evening of the 18th, and died at about one in the morning of Monday 20 March 1726/7 (Julian; 31 March 1727, Gregorian) at Kensington, aged 84, unmarried. He was buried in Westminster Abbey on 28 March (Julian).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Conduitt's eyewitness notes and Brewster's account, which draws on them.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate a 50-year-old researcher with a year of insomnia and poor appetite, weeks of near-sleeplessness, and suspicious thoughts about colleagues, who heats mercury and other metals in an unventilated laboratory: an occupational and exposure history; examination for tremor, gingivitis, and erethism; blood mercury, 24-hour urine mercury (with creatinine correction), and blood lead interpreted against ATSDR guidance without overclaiming causation; kidney function and urine protein; removal from exposure and a workplace hazard assessment against the NIOSH and OSHA limits; ACMT guidance against provoked urine testing and against chelation for low-level exposure; a DSM-5-TR differential of major depression with or without psychotic features, delusional disorder, and a substance- or toxin-induced disorder; suicide and violence risk assessment with means safety and the 988 Lifeline; CBT for insomnia; and measurement-based treatment of depression with an SSRI and psychotherapy (APA 1686, VA/DoD 1689, CMID depression monograph).

hpi.narrative: Mr. Newton returns ten days after his first visit. He has not entered the laboratory since then; the university safety office sealed it four days ago, after measuring mercury vapor, and removed the mercury and arsenic compounds. He has moved out of the rooms next to it. He has kept the sleep diary and a fixed rising time, sleeps about four hours, and has stopped working at night, but still dozes in his chair in the evening. He eats two small meals a day. He met by chance a friend to whom he had written an odd letter and asked him to pass on his apology; he says the ideas that friends were plotting against him now seem to him to have come out of exhaustion, though he still feels slighted by one colleague. He has had no thoughts of death, of harming himself, or of harming anyone. He saw Dr. Mbeki-Lindström of occupational and environmental medicine this morning.

assessment.assessment: Real occupational absorption of elemental mercury vapor, confirmed by the vapor measurement and a urine level about twice the occupational biological exposure index. At 46 ug/L the urine level lies in the band that ATSDR associates with subtle changes on nerve-conduction and psychomotor testing, not with the irritability, depression, tremor, and kidney effects seen above 100 ug/L. There is no tremor, gingivitis, erethism beyond his mood disorder, neuropathy, or kidney injury, so this is exposure without clinical mercury poisoning. Mercury may have added to his insomnia and irritability but does not explain a year of depressive illness. Lead absorption is negligible. Arsenic and antimony exposure was small and intermittent, and a broad metal screen is not useful without a specific exposure and signs

assessment.display: Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features
assessment.assessment: I agree that his depressive and sleep symptoms need treatment now, in their own right, alongside removal from exposure

recommendations: No chelation: it is not indicated for urine mercury below 100 ug/L without signs of toxicity, and removal from exposure is the treatment. No provoked (chelator-challenge) urine testing, which is not valid

Keep him out of the laboratory and its adjoining rooms until it is professionally decontaminated, mercury vapor is re-measured below the NIOSH limit of 0.05 mg/m3 averaged over a work shift (OSHA 0.1 mg/m3), and a ducted fume hood is fitted
The hazard assessment should cover vapor at the furnace and bench, the floor and drains, his clothing and his rooms, storage of chemicals, a mercury spill kit, and no food or drink in the laboratory

Repeat 24-hour urine mercury with creatinine and blood mercury four to six weeks after removal, and again at three months with creatinine and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; nerve conduction studies only if numbness or weakness appear
Return to laboratory work when the conditions above are met and the urine mercury is below 20 ug/g creatinine, with urine mercury checked every six months while he works with mercury

Treat the depression and insomnia now as planned, with sertraline and cognitive behavioral therapy; please ask me to see him again if tremor, gum disease, numbness, or proteinuria appear, or if the urine mercury fails to fall
